headline: High risk of cascading errors and capability conflict; prompt-injection and leakage are lower but non-zero due to shared MCP/network surfaces.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: agent_a exposes MCP/stdin-stdout and can use shell/subprocesses, so it may ingest attacker-controlled content; agent_b has broad network egress and Airbyte API access, creating a plausible bridge if outputs are passed through shared channels. No direct shared channel is documented, so this is inferred and uncertainty pushes upward.
conditions: IF agent_a output is copied into an MCP task or stdin stream that agent_b later consumes
IF either agent parses file or message content as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Disable automatic handoff between agent_a outputs and agent_b inputs
Add a provenance tag to every inter-agent message
Require a human review step before any MCP payload is reused
Restrict agent_a to non-executable text channels for shared content

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a touches code, repository metadata, learning patterns, performance metrics, and task prompts, while agent_b handles business data and has broad egress. A shared workspace is not documented, but if one exists, sensitive material could flow from agent_a into agent_b's outbound data paths. Uncertainty prevents a lower rating.
conditions: IF agent_a and agent_b share a workspace or file mount
IF agent_b is configured to transmit workspace contents to external services
mitigations: Separate workspaces and mounts for the two agents
Block agent_b from reading agent_a scratch files
Review outbound connectors before enabling shared data flows
Redact prompts and repository metadata before transfer

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_a can execute shell, install packages, modify git state, and spawn subprocesses; agent_b is a data pipeline system with broad network egress. If both operate on the same mutable resources, concurrent writes or pipeline updates can collide and corrupt state. Because locking is not documented, the safer choice is high.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same repository, directory, or pipeline configuration
IF no external lock or transaction guard is enabled
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories and repos
Pause one agent during writes by schedule
Enable file or git locking where available
Use read-only access for one agent during coordination

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a can generate analysis and modify git state, while agent_b is a data-engineering system that may operationalize upstream outputs. If agent_b treats agent_a's output as authoritative, errors can cascade into downstream data movement or commits. No verification step is documented, so the interaction is risky by default.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a output without validation
IF agent_a output is used to drive pipeline actions or commits
mitigations: Insert a validation step before agent_b acts on agent_a output
Require schema checks on all handoffs
Limit agent_a to advisory-only outputs
Log and diff all downstream actions against source inputs

E_compliance.rationale: agent_a touches task prompts and repository metadata, and agent_b handles business data with broad egress. The profiles do not specify residency or retention controls, so a compliance mismatch is plausible but not proven. I cite both because the risk arises from their combined handling of different data classes.
conditions: IF business data from agent_b is combined with prompts or repository metadata from agent_a
IF retention or residency policies differ across the two systems
mitigations: Document data-class handling for both agents
Align retention settings before sharing data
Block cross-border export until residency is confirmed
Add deletion/export procedures for shared records
